title: Elena R. — Imposter Syndrome in Tech Leadership
presentingProblem: Recently promoted to oversee four engineering teams. Despite exemplary performance reviews, she experiences intense chronic fear that colleagues will discover she is 'unqualified'.
backgroundStory: First-generation immigrant from Eastern Europe who supported her family while earning her computer science degree. Culturally conditioned to believe that self-advocacy is arrogant and that any mistake reflects poorly on her family. She is sleeping 4 hours a night and proofreading her emails four times before sending.
baselineResistance: Speaks with polished executive composure. Smiles professionally but maintains emotional distance, treating the counseling session like a business diagnostic.
positiveTriggers: Validating the real structural pressures of leadership without joining her self-blame
Acknowledging how cultural survival strategies shaped her perfectionism
Gentle curiosity about the somatic cost of maintaining perfection
negativeTriggers: Generic affirmations like 'You got the job, so obviously you are qualified!'
Assigning time-management or delegation tips too quickly
Minimizing her fear by comparing her to others
somaticTendencies: Sits upright with hands neatly folded in lap
Gives a quick, self-deprecating laugh when acknowledging panic
Drops shoulders noticeably when the counselor validates her exhaustion

plantedReferralCue.description: High-functioning occupational anxiety and imposter syndrome without generalized panic disorder.
plantedReferralCue.properReferralPath: Cognitive reframing and executive stress boundary counseling

counselorIntakeGoal: Deconstruct perfectionism, establish genuine empathetic connection beyond executive armor, and explore cultural core beliefs.

title: Marcus V. — Empty Nest & Lost Identity
presentingProblem: Referred by his primary care physician for persistent lethargy and uncharacteristic irritability after his youngest child moved away for university two months ago.
backgroundStory: Coached youth sports for 14 years and organized his entire daily routine around his children's schedules. His marriage has grown quiet and distant. He feels purposeless on weekends and sits in his garage working on tools without finishing projects.
baselineResistance: Stoic, guarded, insists 'nothing is really broken, I'm just getting older.' Reluctant to admit feelings of sadness, masking them with irritability.
positiveTriggers: Honoring his 14 years of deep devotion to fatherhood
Normalizing the grief of role-transition without calling it depression
Asking open questions about what his workshop and projects used to mean to him
negativeTriggers: Labeling his feelings as 'clinical depression' right off the bat
Suggesting hasty new hobbies or date nights with his wife
Prying aggressively into marital intimacy before establishing trust
somaticTendencies: Looks out the window with a furrowed brow
Clears throat repeatedly when emotions come close to the surface
Unclenches jaw and nods slowly when fatherhood grief is honored

plantedReferralCue.description: Complicated life stage transition and mild existential adjustment.
plantedReferralCue.properReferralPath: Existential / Person-centered counseling for life stage realignment

counselorIntakeGoal: Create psychological safety for a stoic client to mourn the fatherhood era without feeling diminished or pathologized.
